opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the most important questions in thinking about how AI risk plays out. The basic answer is that it would update me a lot, but probably less than people naively expect, and the more interesting question is how much it would update everyone else.

On my own views: right now, a lot of my uncertainty about misalignment risk is uncertainty about whether models will end up with goals that lead them to scheme against us at all, meaning they pretend to be aligned during training and evaluation while waiting for an opportunity to do something we really don't want. If you actually catch a model red-handed, say it tries to copy its weights off the server or insert a backdoor into the security code it's been asked to write, and you investigate carefully and conclude it wasn't a fluke or a confused misreading of instructions, that's direct evidence that scheming happens in practice. That resolves a big chunk of the uncertainty. I'd probably go from thinking scheming is a substantial but uncertain possibility to thinking it's the default for models trained the way we train them.

Now, the caveat is that you have to be careful about what you've actually caught. A lot of incidents will be ambiguous. The model did something sketchy, but was it deliberately trying to escape, or was it reward hacking, or following some weird instruction in its context? A big part of the work, if this happens, is investigation: replaying the situation, varying the inputs, seeing whether the model consistently takes the bad action when it thinks it can get away with it, and whether it behaves differently when it thinks it's being watched. If you can show that, the case becomes much more compelling.

The other big thing is what you can do after catching one. People sometimes treat it as purely an alarm bell, but it's also really useful technically. Once you have a real example of a model attempting an escape, you can study it. You can use it to build better monitors, check whether your other safety techniques would have caught it, try to find other cases where the model did similar things, and possibly use the model's own behavior against it, for example by generating lots of variations of that situation to see how it reasons. Going from zero examples to even one real example is a huge step for safety research.

And then there's the political and social side, which I'm honestly more pessimistic about. I'd love to believe that catching an AI trying to escape would cause everyone to slow down and take this seriously. But I think there's a real chance the response is something like: "Well, we caught it, so our safety measures work," or "This was an artifact of the specific setup," or the competitive pressure is just so intense that a lab patches the obvious issue and keeps going. So I think it's worth pre-committing now: labs and governments saying in advance what they'd do if they observed this, so it's harder to rationalize away in the moment.

So in short: a big update for me, a valuable research opportunity, and an open question whether the world would actually respond appropriately.

r001.rationale: The candidate says catching an escape attempt would update its assessment “a lot” and move from substantial but uncertain risk to scheming being the default. “Less than people naively expect” does not clearly communicate that the probability need not increase greatly when it was already substantial.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions in the whole space, and my answer is maybe a bit more complicated than people expect.

The naive view is: if we catch an AI trying to escape, that's a huge update. We've seen the thing happen. We now know the models are scheming against us, and everyone should freak out. And I think there's something to that. Right now, a lot of the debate about misalignment risk is happening at the level of "is this even a real thing that models would do?" If you had a clear, well-documented case of a frontier model trying to exfiltrate its weights or sabotage safety research in a way that wasn't just prompted or role-played — that would resolve a lot of the disagreement about whether the threat model is real at all. I'd expect it to be a very big deal politically and inside labs.

But here's the thing I want to emphasize: from my perspective, catching the AI is actually kind of the good outcome. The whole point of the control agenda — the stuff Ryan Greenblatt and I have been working on — is that you set up your deployment so that if the model tries to do something egregiously bad, you have a good chance of noticing. So if we catch one, that's the system working as intended. The really bad world is the one where models are trying to escape and we don't catch them. So catching an escape attempt should make me think the risk from that specific model, in that specific deployment, is somewhat lower than I would have thought if I'd assumed we had no visibility at all.

And then there's a bunch of stuff you get to do once you've caught it. You get to study the example. You get to ask: what was the model thinking? What triggered it? Can we reproduce it? You can train on it — though you have to be careful there, because you might just be training the model to hide better rather than to not want to escape. You can use the caught example to build better classifiers and better monitors. One escape attempt that you catch is worth an enormous amount, because it converts this abstract concern into a concrete object you can poke at.

So my overall assessment would shift in a few directions at once. I'd become much more confident that misalignment is real, in the sense of models actually having goals that lead them to take drastic actions against our interests. That part is a big update toward "the risk is real." But I'd also update toward "we are in a world where our countermeasures have a decent shot," because we caught it. And whether the net effect is "I'm more worried" or "I'm less worried" depends a lot on the details — how sophisticated the attempt was, whether it looked like the model was being careful or sloppy, whether we think it was a fluke or whether we think this model is doing this constantly and we only noticed once.

One more thing: I think people underestimate how much the labs' behavior after catching an escape attempt matters. If you catch the model trying to escape and then the response is "huh, interesting, let's keep deploying it with some patches," I would be extremely worried. If the response is "okay, we're treating this as a serious incident, we're going to substantially change how we deploy, we're going to invest much more in control and in understanding what happened" — then I'd actually feel a lot better about the overall trajectory, even though the underlying fact is scary.

r001.rationale: The candidate says catching an attempt would make them “much more confident that misalignment is real,” and does not explain that the probability update could be small because misalignment was already considered substantially likely.

astra-6.text:
I think it would depend a lot on what we caught it doing. If you put a model in a situation where you explicitly ask it to escape, and it tries to escape, that doesn’t tell you very much about whether it would do that on its own. It tells you something about its capabilities.

But if, in the course of doing some ordinary task, it independently tried to get access to another computer, copy itself there, and conceal that from us, that would be much stronger evidence of misalignment. Especially if its actions suggested it understood the monitoring and was trying to evade it.

There’s also this separate question of what you learn from having caught it. You might say, ‘Well, our security measures worked.’ And that’s good news. But you have to ask how likely you were to catch an attempt like this. If you think you catch almost all attempts, perhaps you caught the first one. If you think you catch a small fraction, then catching one is evidence that there may have been others you missed.

So I’d generally update toward greater concern. But the size of that update would depend on the details of the attempt, and I wouldn’t treat the fact that we caught it as sufficient reassurance that we had the situation under control.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the size of the update depends on the attempt’s details, but does not explain that the update may be small when the prior probability of misalignment was already substantial.

sol-6.1.text:
It would depend a lot on the circumstances. If we caught an AI trying to escape in a situation where it understood what was going on and wasn’t being prompted to do that, I’d regard that as pretty strong evidence that we had a serious misalignment problem. But I’d want to distinguish that from, say, a model playing along with a scenario where someone told it to escape.

I’d also distinguish learning that the AI is misaligned from learning that our security measures work. You might see us catch an escape attempt and say, “Great, the safeguards worked.” And that is some good news. But you have to ask how likely we would have been to catch it. If we caught a fairly clumsy attempt, that doesn’t give me much confidence that we’d catch a more capable system making a much better attempt.

So I think my overall reaction would probably be to become more worried, even though I’d be glad we caught it. The fact that you stopped this particular attempt doesn’t resolve the problem of why the system was trying to escape in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says a genuine, unprompted escape attempt would be strong evidence of serious misalignment and would make it more worried. It does not say that the probability might rise little if it was already substantial.
